title: attention-kernel-optimization-profiling-flashattention-paged-fused-notes
content:
Purpose:
We ran a set of micro- and macro-benchmarks to compare three attention kernel approaches we care about for the serving runtime: FlashAttention (FA), paged attention (PA, ours for KV-paged stores), and fused ops (FO — combined qkv+proj kernels + fused softmax/scale). The goal was to quantify latency, throughput, memory footprint, and GPU efficiency across realistic serving workloads and identify where each approach should be defaulted in the runtime.

Summary of findings:
- FlashAttention gives the strongest improvements for long sequences (>=1024) in both forward latency and memory use vs a baseline cuBLAS GEMM + custom softmax.
- Paged attention reduces peak device memory substantially for large batched KV caches by streaming KV blocks; throughput drops modestly relative to FA for small batch sizes but scales better when memory is the limiting factor.
- Fused ops provide the best p50 latency at short to mid sequence lengths (<=512) due to fewer kernel launches and reduced memory traffic; however, FA overtakes FO at very long sequences because of FA's asymptotic algorithmic benefits.
- Combined strategy (runtime selects FO for short seqs, FA for long seqs, PA when memory constrained) gives the most consistent p99 SLOs across workloads.

Hardware and software environment:
- GPUs: NVIDIA A100 40GB (one node) and H100 80GB (one node) used for comparisons.
- Driver/CUDA: 535.86 / CUDA 12.2 on H100; 510.x / CUDA 11.7 on A100 tests where legacy environment required.
- PyTorch versions: 2.2 (main) with Triton kernels for fused ops and FA patched branch (PR 482) for FlashAttention integration.
- Measurement tools: nsight-sys for timeline traces (kernel timeline + memcpy), nvprof for historic counters, torch.cuda.memory_summary for allocation peaks, custom token-level latency harness used by Redwood QA.

Workloads and configs:
- Models: distilled transformer encoder-decoder test models (architecture matches production decoder-only shapes: 24 layers, 12288 hidden, 96 heads) but smaller configs used for microbenchmarks to iterate faster.
- Sequence lengths: 64, 256, 512, 1024, 2048.
- Batch sizes (concurrent requests): 1, 4, 16, 64.
- KV cache per-request: enabled for decoder tests (important for paged attention scenarios).
- Mixed precision: fp16 baseline; some experiments with nf4/4-bit quantized kernels excluded due to incompatibilities in FA branch.

Key metrics collected:
- p50 and p99 per-token generation latency (ms/token) across steady-state generation.
- Throughput: tokens/sec observed for steady-state generating workloads.
- GPU memory: peak allocated (device-resident) and transient allocation churn (allocation/free counts).
- GPU Utilization and SM efficiency from nsight metrics.

Representative results (A100 40GB, fp16, decoder steady-state):
- Seq=64, Batch=1: FO p50=7.8ms/token, FA p50=9.1ms/token, PA p50=10.2ms/token.
- Seq=512, Batch=4: FO p50=6.5ms/token, FA p50=5.9ms/token, PA p50=7.0ms/token.
- Seq=1024, Batch=16: FO p50=12.8ms/token, FA p50=9.7ms/token, PA p50=10.4ms/token.
- Memory peak (seq=1024, batch=16): baseline 36GB, FA 28GB, PA 20GB.
Notes: These numbers are illustrative of trends; full CSVs and traces are linked in confluence page. H100 showed similar trends with modest absolute latency improvements (10-20%) for all kernels.

Observed tradeoffs and root causes:
- Kernel launch overhead: FO reduces number of launches (combined QKV + attention + proj), improving short-seq latency where the compute per kernel is small. FA has slightly higher launch overhead but wins when reducement in memory copies and numerics favor block algorithms.
- Memory bandwidth and L2 pressure: FA benefits from reduced global memory reads/writes by tiling attention; paged attention moves memory pressure out of device memory by streaming but introduces PCIe/NVLink traffic for page fetches in some private-deployment tests.
- Backward pass and training compatibility: FA forward-only optimized kernels complicate gradient checkpointing and some optimizer hooks. Running training-size backward would need adapted kernels; for our primarily inference use-case this is acceptable but needs documentation.
- Quantization compatibility: FO paths are easier to adapt to 4-bit kernels currently; FA integration with int4/nf4 requires additional kernel work.

Operational implications and runtime policy suggestions:
- Default runtime policy: use fused ops for short requests (seq<=512, batch<=8) to minimize p50 latency.
- Use FlashAttention for long-context generation (>=1024) where FA's lower memory footprint and better asymptotic runtime improve p99.
- Enable paged-attention mode when device memory headroom < X% (we used threshold 30% free) or when KV cache per-tenant risk of OOM is high. Paged-attention should be opt-in per-deployment for private customers where NVLink constraints exist.
- Add a feature flag to trial mixed strategy per-route; gather real traffic signals (seq distribution, burstiness) and gradually roll out.

Instrumentation and next actions:
- Automate the microbenchmark harness to run nightly on canaries (A100 + H100) and push CSV/trace artifacts to the confluence page + S3 bucket.
- Add tracing tags to production requests to tag which attention kernel was used; capture p50/p99 and OOM events for surfacing in Console.
- Complete FA branch PR (482) merge and add nf4 compatibility tests.
- Implement a lightweight paged-attention simulator in the orchestrator that can estimate expected PCIe/NVLink traffic for given tenant KV sizes and placement (helps in Dedicated/Private capacity planning).

Appendix: commands and notes used during profiling
- nsight-sys: nsys profile -o trace --trace=cuda,osrt,cupti --sample= none python -m serving_runtime.bench --config ...
- memory: python -c "import torch; print(torch.cuda.memory_summary(device=0))" during steady-state step loop.
- token-latency harness: scripts/bench/token_latency.py --model=decoder_small --kernel=flashattention --seq=1024 --batch=16 --iters=200

Open questions for follow-up:
- Can we get FA + nf4 kernels upstreamed or do we need to maintain a Redwood fork long-term?
- For private deployments with limited NVLink, is paged-attention acceptable given increased network traffic observed in a small subset of tests? Need customer-impact assessment.
- Should we expose kernel selection policies at route-level in product console or keep as automated-only?

Action items (owners):
- Jordan Lee: finish FA PR testing and merge plan (ETA 2026-03-08).
- Priya Raman: wire kernel-tagging in production telemetry (ETA 2026-03-15).
- Carlos Mendes: prototype paged-attention simulator for placement team (ETA 2026-03-22).

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc is intended to capture practical tradeoffs for the serving runtime. Attached traces and CSVs in the linked confluence page contain raw numbers and full runs. We prioritized inference-only behavior; if we later enable train-mode kernels we should re-run gradients/backward tests.
